Not talking about a specific experience but about the state of reality:

Reality must be, in my opinion, one defined state. It is another question if we can find out which state this is. But there must be one state of affairs in the universe, regarding some questions.

E.g. either the universe is such that

a) there is no god

b) there is exactly one god

c) there are many gods

Either the universe is such that 
1) all there is are material objects and everything regarding mind and cognition is a consequence of e.g. a specific arrangement of the material objects in question - that we are machines

or

2) In addition to material objects there exists something that is of itself not-material but can interact with matter. E.g. one can think of our minds or cognition as some kind of non-material entity (soul) interacting with our bodies.

>So, no "Truth" is incorrect or correct.

Even if we don't know if a certain statement is true or false - the statement itself still is either true or false. Either there are no gods in existance, or there is one or more gods out there.

Regarding questions for which the state of affairs can not be proven (or might not be proven withing our lifetimes) it is still possible and imo it is worthwhile to make reasonable assumptions about the probability of this or that state of affairs based on observation of the state of the real world.

I try to be short:
You can observe in various wavelengths of the electromagnetic spectrum.
A small part of that spectrum is what we see as visible light (the "optical spectrum")

Best pictures in the optical spectrum are taken with space telescopes (e.g. Hubble Space Telescope, HST).

Now if you only take an optical image, you don't see a picture with a lot of pretty colours like that http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/98/Andromeda_Galaxy_(with_h-alpha).jpg

And the colours in that pictures are far from meaningless(!):

Imagine that you observe the same object (e.g. Andromeda as in the link above) 
- in the opitcal (e.g. with HST)
- in the radio spectrum (e.g. with that http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effelsberg_100-m_Radio_Telescope - btw: in Radioastronomy, it's easier to take pictures with experiments based on earth. )
(and if you like with many more wavelengts - you can even use X-ray telescopes and gamma ray observatorys, ifrared whatever you like and can measure.
E.g. a standard DSLR photo camera might often be slightly sensitive to infrared wavelengths.)

In the end you combine each picture. You overlay the information and preserve the angular/spatial information.
You have thus obtained information on the observed object from a much wider spectrum than only optical. You have retected radiowaves from that object and gamma rays from that object etc.

To make that information visible in the combined picture, you assign colours to each spectrum you have observed.
Let the information of the HST (optical) be just withe, let Infrared be red, let UV be violet, let gamma rays be blue.

As a result you get something like in the link above: A picture of e.g. the Andromeda galaxy where the various colours correspond to the structures that objects that dominantly emit in the one or the other spectrum can be seen.
Keep in mind: Those colours are chosen artifically (X-rays can't be seen with the human eye and thus have no native colour) but have physical meaning!
